change.describe: branch `pr-80329-flat` of grafana-80329-flat against a886bd3c79a417a70b51509384d1f1ec3e87e96b (merge-base a886bd3)
change.title: pr-80329-flat
change.author: Cristian Sotomayor

findings.title: Debug logging left in at Error level, with every ID in the batch
findings.body: Six `r.log.Error(...)` calls (lines 534, 537, 554, 557, 576, 579) run on every batch of every cleanup cycle, including successful ones and empty batches. Each call logs the full `ids` slice: 100 IDs at the default `cleanupjob_batchsize` (pkg/setting/setting.go:710), and up to tens of thousands for large batch sizes. They also log `err`, which is always nil on lines 534/554/576 because the error was already returned above. Error-level output fires alerting and floods logs while nothing is wrong. Remove these calls, or turn them into one `Debug` line per run with counts only.

findings.title: Cleanup interval changed from 10 minutes to 1 minute
findings.body: This looks like a leftover from local testing. The ticker drives every cleanup job (snapshots, dashboard versions, images, annotations, invites, short URLs, query history; lines 96-105), so they now run 10× as often. The 9-minute timeout at line 89 was sized to fit inside the 10-minute interval. With a 1-minute ticker, a long run is followed straight away by another, so cleanup runs almost continuously. That works against a PR titled "Database Performance Optimizations". Restore `time.Minute * 10`.

findings.title: Quadratic string building for inlined SQLite IDs
findings.body: `values = fmt.Sprintf("%s, %d", values, v)` copies the whole string built so far on every iteration, so the cost is O(n²) in the batch size. This branch only runs when the batch size is above 999. At the 32767 batch size the new test uses, that is roughly 32767²/2 × ~7 bytes ≈ several GB of copying per DELETE, repeated for every batch and for the tag cleanup too. Build the list with `strings.Builder` or with `strconv.FormatInt` plus `strings.Join`.

findings.title: Placeholder count is unbounded on MySQL/Postgres
findings.body: On every driver except SQLite with batch size > 999, the DELETE gets one `?` per ID. PostgreSQL and MySQL prepared statements both cap bound parameters at 65535. So with `cleanupjob_batchsize` set above 65535, every batch now fails and annotation cleanup stops entirely: the error is returned from `CleanAnnotations` and only logged by `cleanUpOldAnnotations` (pkg/services/cleanup/cleanup.go:126-127). The old single-statement subquery had no such limit. Either cap the chunk size used in `deleteByIDs`, or inline the integer IDs for these drivers too (as the SQLite branch does).

findings.title: Test case no longer runs the delete "again"
findings.body: Each subtest now creates fresh data and wipes it in `t.Cleanup`. This case therefore no longer re-runs the max-count cleanup on state the previous case left behind; it just creates 9 annotations (3 per type) with MaxCount 3. It is still a valid check, but the name now describes a scenario that isn't tested. Either rename it, or run `cleaner.Run` twice inside one subtest to keep the idempotency check.

findings.title: Cleanup registered after the setup assertions
findings.body: `t.Cleanup` is registered only after `createTestAnnotations` and the two count assertions have passed. If any of them fails via `require` (FailNow), the rows already inserted stay in the shared `fakeSQL`. Every later subtest then fails on its initial count assertion, which hides the real failure. Register the cleanup before inserting.

contracts.action: CleanAnnotations / CleanOrphanedAnnotationTags now SELECT ids, then DELETE ... WHERE id IN (ids) in a separate session
contracts.equivalent_path: Previous single statement DELETE ... WHERE id IN (SELECT id FROM (SELECT ... LIMIT) a), run by executeUntilDoneOrCancelled
contracts.before_after: Old: selection and delete happened atomically in one statement. New: the IDs are fetched in one session (fetchIDs, lines 584-595) and deleted in another (deleteByIDs, lines 621-628). Nothing re-checks the condition at delete time. MaxAge: `created` of an existing row does not move forward, so the fetched rows still match. Orphan tags: an annotation_id that is missing cannot reappear, because IDs are not reused. MaxCount: if newer annotations are deleted concurrently between fetch and delete, a fetched row may now fall inside the kept MaxCount window and be over-deleted. That is bounded by the number of concurrent deletions, and only rows that were already candidates for count-based eviction are affected.
contracts.visible_effect: Annotations disappear from dashboards on the cleanup cycle; the counts reach the cleanup job's Debug log (cleanup.go:129).
contracts.failure_mode: A fetch or delete error returns from untilDoneOrCancelled (lines 650-654) with a partial total. cleanUpOldAnnotations logs it at Error unless it is DeadlineExceeded (cleanup.go:126-127). No journal is involved, so the next cycle retries. If a delete affects 0 rows (rows already gone), the loop stops early and the next cycle picks up the rest.

contracts.action: deleteByIDs chooses inline IDs vs placeholders based on DB type and configured batch size
contracts.equivalent_path: Old subquery DELETE had no bound parameters
contracts.before_after: SQLite with batch size > 999 inlines the int64 IDs; no injection risk, because they are integers formatted with %d. Every other case binds one placeholder per ID, which is unbounded for MySQL/Postgres.
contracts.visible_effect: If parameter limits are exceeded, cleanup silently stops removing annotations; the only trace is an error log.
contracts.failure_mode: On Postgres/MySQL, a batch size above 65535 makes every DELETE fail (reported as a finding).

contracts.action: Cleanup ticker interval reduced to 1 minute
contracts.equivalent_path: Previous 10-minute ticker, paired with the 9-minute timeout in clean()
contracts.before_after: clean() runs all 8 jobs with a 9-minute timeout (lines 89-118). time.Ticker drops ticks while clean() is busy, so a long run is followed by another almost immediately.
contracts.visible_effect: More DB load from background cleanup; expired snapshots and short URLs are removed sooner.

summary: The PR splits annotation and orphan-tag cleanup into two steps: fetch the IDs, then delete them in a batch. The deletes are safe because their targets cannot change meaning between the two steps; the one exception is a small, bounded over-delete under concurrent deletes on the max-count path. Three things should be fixed. It leaves six Error-level debug log calls that print every ID on every batch. It changes the global cleanup interval from 10 minutes to 1, which looks like a leftover from testing. And it builds the inlined SQLite ID list in quadratic time. Also, MySQL/Postgres now bind one placeholder per ID, so a batch size above 65535 makes every cleanup DELETE fail. In the tests, one case name no longer matches what it tests, and the per-subtest cleanup is registered too late to stop failures cascading into later subtests.
